spans.text: Based on Hoffmann et al.’s report of having “over 400” observations, we interpret this to mean they likely had between 400 and 500 data points. If, as they claimed, they used only the final loss values for each trained model, it seems unlikely that they would have had hundreds of thousands of observations.

Second, the scaling policy derived from Hoffmann et al.’s estimated parameters suggests using approximately 70 tokens per parameter for optimal performance. This prescription is inconsistent with the 20 tokens-per-parameter ratio actually used by Hoffmann et al. to train their 70B Chinchilla model.

A few datapoints stand out. There is a column of points with training FLOP around where some of the larger models obtain high loss values (up to 70% higher compared to models with similar compute budgets). These correspond to the lowest ratio of training tokens to parameters
Farseer demonstrates a fourfold reduction in relative prediction error compared to Chinchilla at large scale (0.50% versus 2.68% at 25B parameters)

Farseer predicts that the optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio grows with compute, matching observed behavior in recent LLMs (e.g., Llama 3, Qwen3), and offers a robust proxy for evaluating new architecture and data recipes at small scale.

The honest caveat: scaling laws fit to pretraining loss may not predict downstream task performance. The loss-downstream divergence is most pronounced when the evaluation task is far from the pretraining distribution.

claims.text: The Hoffmann et al. published Chinchilla scaling law coefficients have confidence intervals approximately 50-fold narrower than the ~400 data points would statistically justify; replication studies estimate 80% confidence intervals of ±0.09 compared to the reported ±0.002, suggesting the true optimal token-per-parameter ratio spans from roughly 4 to 40 across reasonable regimes rather than being precisely 20. This uncertainty directly affects capex planning—a 70B model budget could validly support anywhere from 280B to 2.8T tokens.

claims.text: The optimal token-per-parameter ratio depends materially on training data quality: higher-quality or filtered datasets achieve identical loss improvements at ratios below 20× (Bi et al. 2024 found lower ratios optimal for higher-quality data), meaning investments in data curation deliver compounding returns across your model portfolio proportional to model size. This explains divergence between Chinchilla's three independent estimation methods—they implicitly used different data quality controls.

claims.text: The Hoffmann et al. paper reports 80% confidence intervals of ±0.001 for the optimal token-per-parameter scaling exponent, but bootstrap reanalysis shows standard errors 50 times wider (±0.018). Obtaining intervals that tight would require nearly 600,000 experiments; the authors likely ran only 400–500. Their Approach 3 fit is statistically rejected against their own data (p < 0.001) and contradicts their Approaches 1 & 2—Approach 3 prescribes ~70 tokens per parameter, while their actual Chinchilla model trains at 20 and Approaches 1 & 2 support ~20.

claims.text: Llama-3 8B trained at ~1875 tokens-per-parameter and frontier models in 2025 train at 1000+ tokens-per-parameter—roughly 50–100× above Chinchilla's compute-optimal ratio of 20. This inference-optimal strategy costs more in training but reduces per-token serving cost; at billion-request scale, training amortizes to <1% of total lifetime cost. Smaller models with longer training reach identical loss as larger compute-optimal models but at much lower inference cost, making the overtraining tradeoff economically rational for any production deployment with >100 million requests.

claims.text: Scaling laws predict pretraining loss on web text but not instruction-tuned downstream accuracy, which saturates earlier and scales noisily. A 10% perplexity reduction may improve coding accuracy 20% but summarization only 3%. MoE models, fine-tuned models, and specialized architectures (rerankers, embeddings) break the simple power-law fit entirely. Loss-downstream divergence is most pronounced when the evaluation task lies far from the pretraining distribution.
